reason: The sources provide 20 distinct claims with support from multiple independent sites, offering a complete narrative arc with a surprising scientific twist.
story: In 1960, NASA launched one of the most bizarre-looking spacecraft in history: Project Echo. It wasn't a complex computer, but a 100-foot-wide balloon made of shiny, aluminum-coated Mylar. Nicknamed the 'satelloon,' it was launched folded into a small canister and inflated once it reached orbit. Its job was to act as a giant mirror in the sky, reflecting radio signals between ground stations. Because it was massive and highly reflective, it became the first man-made object easily visible to the naked eye, appearing brighter than most stars. It relayed the first satellite phone calls and TV broadcasts, proving global satellite communication was possible. However, the mission’s most famous achievement happened by accident. A massive horn-shaped antenna built at Bell Labs to listen to Echo's faint reflections accidentally picked up a persistent hiss. This noise turned out to be the 'echo' of the Big Bang, a discovery that won the Nobel Prize.
angle: NASA's first communication satellite was a giant, 100-foot-wide shiny balloon that was so bright it was mistaken for a star by millions on Earth.

claims.claim: Project Echo was NASA's first passive communications satellite experiment.
The Echo 1 satellite was a giant inflatable sphere measuring approximately 100 feet (30.5 meters) in diameter.
The satellite was constructed from thin Mylar polyester film.
The Mylar was coated or laminated with aluminum to make it reflective.
Echo 1 was launched into space in 1960.
Echo 1A was successfully launched on August 12, 1960, from Cape Canaveral.
The spacecraft was nicknamed a 'satelloon' by project personnel.
The balloon was visible to the unaided eye from the ground and appeared brighter than most stars.
It functioned as a passive reflector that bounced signals from one point on Earth to another.
The satellite relayed the first satellite telephone, radio, and television signals.
The balloon was inflated in orbit after leaving the atmosphere.
Sublimating powders, including benzoic acid, were used to maintain internal pressure and shape.
Echo 2 was launched in 1964 and was larger than Echo 1 at 135 feet (41.1 meters) in diameter.
The project was a collaboration involving NASA, Bell Telephone Laboratories, and the Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
The giant horn antenna at Holmdel, built for Echo, led to the discovery of cosmic microwave background radiation.
Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson won the Nobel Prize in Physics for their discovery made with the Echo antenna.
Echo 1 and Echo 2 were used to study atmospheric drag and solar pressure.
Echo 1A reentered the Earth's atmosphere and burned up in May 1968.
The U.S. Post Office issued a postage stamp depicting Echo 1 in 1960.
The satellites proved that microwave transmissions to and from space were feasible.

disputed: Launch Mass: S1 states the launch weight was 157 lb (71 kg), while S3 states it was 76 kg. A script should use 'approximately 160 pounds.'
Test Dates: S1 lists the first Shotput test on October 27, 1959, while S3 lists October 28, 1959. A script should attribute this to 'late October 1959.'

Mylar Thickness: S3 claims the Mylar was 0.5 mm thick, while S1 and S2 specify 12.7 micrometers (0.0127 mm). S3's figure is significantly larger; a script should follow S1 and S2 or say 'thinner than human hair.'
